implementerProof.how: Round 3: I re-ran both of this round's production-like proofs at my own build of this head — `workspace-init provision` with the branch deleted from the feed, and `legion start --check-config` on an example I staged — and both hold. addedTest.why: Not a defect — the code is right — but an invariant of this round's fix that nothing in the package held. The runtime keeps the replaced pod's uid under the Sandbox's name while a migrating launch has deleted the Sandbox and not yet created its replacement, and `evaluate` compares that kept uid with the locator's before calling an end displaced. Dropping the comparison (`stranded = held != ""`) leaves the **whole sandbox package green**, measured against a baseline I first made green — the three repository files its tests read by relative path symlinked beside my out-of-tree copy, after which `go test ./internal/runtime/sandbox` is `ok`. Without the comparison, a role recorded in an earlier pod of the same issue that ends on its own inside that gap is read as the daemon's own replacement and resumed uncharged: a death the supervisor never counts and a failing role nothing ever stops. The new test probes exactly that locator inside the gap and requires Gone and not Displaced. It passes at this head and fails with the comparison dropped, naming the pod it was wrongly told was displaced.
addedTest.evidence: `go test ./internal/runtime/sandbox -run TestAGapReadOfARoleOfAnotherPodThanTheReplacementEndedIsNotDisplaced` — PASS at this head; with `held == loc.Sandbox.PodUID` removed from `evaluate`, FAIL: `a role recorded in pod uid-pod-older, read in the gap the replacement of pod uid-pod-old opened: gone, Displaced true …; want Gone and not Displaced`.

proof.criterion: The cutover's displacement window: a sibling role read while the issue has no Sandbox at all is the daemon's own end, not a death.
proof.surface: The package's own rig — the real `relaunch`, `evaluate` and `Probe` paths against an httptest API server — driven as a defect reproduction: the fix reverted in an out-of-tree copy, the failure observed, the fix restored, green again.
proof.command: In /tmp/mods/daemon (a copy of packages/daemon at this head): drop the `case current == nil: stranded = …` arm from `evaluate` and run `go test ./internal/runtime/sandbox -run 'TestASiblingReadBetweenAMigratingLaunchsDeleteAndCreateIsDisplaced|TestAReplacementWhoseCreateFailsKeepsTheReplacedPodsRolesDisplaced'`; restore and re-run
proof.observed: Without the fix both fail, and they name the two shapes of the window: `the reviewer recorded in the replaced pod, read while no Sandbox of the issue exists: gone, Displaced false (sandbox legion/legion-legion-legion-208 is absent); want Gone and Displaced`, and the same after the replacement's Create was refused — the second being the window a failed Create holds open until the issue's next launch, not the instant a successful one takes. Both pass at this head. Since a Gone delivered leaves the watch, a death read here is a death that cannot be taken back by the annotation arriving a moment later, which is what makes this the cutover's own failure mode rather than a transient.
proof.negativeControl: The third of this round's tests, run unmodified: once the replacement carries the name, the record is dropped and a role of the replacement's **own** pod that ends on its own is a death, not a displacement. Dropping the `unstrand` call instead makes `TestTheNameAReplacementKeptForItsGapGoesOnceTheReplacementCarriesIt` fail, so the keeping is bounded at both ends and not merely added.

proof.criterion: 1. The rendered pods, this round's controller pod among them, are what a real API server accepts against the pinned Agent Sandbox definition.
proof.surface: A real Kubernetes API server, v1.37 (etcd and kube-apiserver from the envtest assets, run in this pod), with the pinned production Agent Sandbox CRD applied and the daemon's own goldens submitted to it — the schema walker's conclusion taken from the thing it reproduces.
proof.command: `kubectl apply -f testdata/sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io.yaml`, then `kubectl create -f` each of `testdata/golden/{worker,controller,controller-resume}.json` under a name of my own, then read each back
proof.observed: All three accepted. The issue pod comes back with its six role containers, its two init containers, its disk an `ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate` with empty metadata, and its Sandbox owning no claim template. The controller's pod comes back with its one `controller` container, **no `initContainers` key at all** — this round's deletion of the emptied init container, which a schema requiring the field would have refused — and its disk the `issue` claim its own Sandbox owns. So the two kinds differ on a real API server exactly where the change says they differ.
proof.negativeControl: Round 2's, on the same surface and unchanged since: a label on the issue pod's ephemeral claim template is pruned (201, stored metadata `{}`, with a `warning: 299` header) by a client that sets no field validation and refused outright by a strict one, and `spec.volumeClaimTemplates` on a live Sandbox is refused `volumeClaimTemplates is immutable` — the premise of the cutover's delete-and-create.

proof.criterion: 2. An issue whose branch has been merged and deleted starts its agents — re-verified at this head.

A labelled claim template is pruned — 201 with stored metadata `{}` and a `warning: 299` header. `volumeClaimTemplates is immutable` on a live Sandbox. The suspension's merge patch returns 200 carrying `{"legion.dev/displaced-pod": "uid-pod-old"}` in its own response, which is what the round-1 fix reads, and the replacement carrying that annotation is accepted.

proof.criterion: The round-2 correctness fixes: the replacement carries the displaced-pod name, and an init container the daemon's own delete killed is not a failed init.

Without the annotation carry, `the Sandbox this launch created names "" as the pod the daemon replaced, want uid-pod-old`. Both pass restored.

proof.criterion: 1. The disk is created with its pod and deleted with it, at today's size and storage.
proof.surface: A real Kubernetes cluster — the build namespace this worker pod may submit Jobs to admits exactly the volume shape this change renders — running a pod that declares the same `ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate` the issue goldens show, with the namespace's claim counter as the observation Legion's own tests cannot make. The issue pod's volume block is byte-identical from that head to this one, checked with `jj diff --from b650d854 --to @-` over `podkind.go`, `manifest.go` and all three issue goldens, so the measurement carries.
proof.command: `kubectl apply -f` the Job, poll `kubectl get resourcequota … persistentvolumeclaims` through the pod's life, read the pod's own `spec.volumes[0]` and its log, then `kubectl delete job`
proof.observed: The claim counter went 0 → 1 while the pod was still **Pending**; the disk came up holding `lost+found` alone with 19.5G free and took a 16 MiB write; the counter **stayed at 1 after the pod reached Completed**, so the claim's life is the pod object's and not the container's; and it was back to 0 about **one second** after the pod was deleted.
proof.negativeControl: The same Job with one label on that claim template was refused by the namespace's admission policy naming the rule.

proof.criterion: 6. The upgrade half of the cutover: an issue_suspend row the running release queued must still run after the upgrade.
proof.surface: A real PostgreSQL 16 run as a workload in the cluster, carrying the daemon's own schema, driven by the daemon's own migration runner and enqueue path, with the payload bytes `json.Marshal` produces from `record.IssueSuspend` as the previous release declares it. Migration 0051 and that struct are untouched since.
proof.command: migrate; delete the schema_version row for 51; enqueue the two rows that release writes, one mid-retry; decode each; `store.Migrate` again; decode again
proof.observed: At schema 50 the head binary refuses the releasing row — `json: unknown field "release"` — the stall the migration prevents, reproduced. The upgrade applied exactly 1 migration. Both rows then decode, with attempts, next_at, last_error and created_at byte-identical, so a row mid-retry keeps its backoff.

proof.criterion: 5. No code is left that reuses, repairs or inspects a disk from an earlier pod, with the stale git-lock sweep kept for the retry on the same disk.
proof.surface: The tree, plus the one runtime surface where a provision can still meet a non-empty disk: the kubelet restarts a failed init container in the same pod.
proof.command: the deletion grep, then `provision` into a root it had already provisioned after planting this issue's own production failure signature (`refs/jj/keep/badref`)
proof.observed: 17 hits, all history or negative assertions. With the planted bad ref, provision exits 1 in 0.98 s with `fatal: bad object refs/jj/keep/badref` — no repair attempted, no hang, which is what leaves the pod replaceable.
proof.negativeControl: With four stale git locks planted instead, the same command removed each by name and exited 0.

coverageInventory.question: For each behaviour this change inverts in the live Stage 4a proof, what covers it without a cluster, what run #1 already covered, and what only a live run can show. Asked by the architect at 10:33Z because the rerun may not happen before the merge.
provenWithoutACluster: The rendered pod's shape survives the API server, not merely a golden: the issue pod's disk is an ephemeral claim template with empty metadata and its Sandbox owns none, accepted unchanged by a real kube-apiserver v1.37 against the pinned CRD, with a labelled template pruned and `volumeClaimTemplates` refused as immutable (round 2 proof, re-run this round with the controller goldens).

A generic ephemeral claim of this shape is created with its pod, outlives the container, and is reaped about a second after the pod object goes — measured on a real cluster of this deployment, on the same storage class (round 1 proof). This is the Kubernetes mechanism the change rests on; what it does not include is Legion's own pod creating it.
A deployment cannot configure the file session store, at the loader and again at `sandbox.New` (rounds 2 and 3).
An issue whose branch was merged and deleted provisions onto the default branch, on the real binary and a real repository (every round).

**No lost-volume line anywhere in the daemon's log.** This one can be moved out of the live-only group outright: the code that wrote it is deleted, which the deletion grep and its negative control show. A live run can only fail to observe a line nothing can emit; the tree is the stronger evidence, and the live assertion is a belt on braces.
coveredByLiveRunOne: The Agent Sandbox controller passes a generic ephemeral pod volume through untouched: the claim `<pod>-issue` created by `kube-system:ephemeral-volume-controller`, owned by the pod with `controller: true`, differing from the template only in the defaulted `volumeMode: Filesystem`. I checked the architect's caveat myself: the issue pod's volume block is byte-identical between `b650d854`, the head that ran, and this head — `podkind.go`, `manifest.go` and all three issue goldens — so the observation carries.
liveOnlyAndUnproven: **The disk actually going when Legion's pod goes.** Both halves are observed — the claim is pod-owned with `controller: true` (run #1) and a pod-owned claim of this shape is reaped about a second after its pod (round 1, real cluster) — and Kubernetes' garbage collector follows exactly that ownership. What no evidence here composes is the two in one run on Legion's own pod. Judge it as a composition of two observed facts rather than an open question, which is weaker than a live run and much stronger than nothing.

**A re-admitted issue coming back on a disk of its own**, in the sense the check makes: two claim uids compared across a pod replacement. Nothing without a cluster can produce a claim uid. The half that is covered is that the replacement pod is created and provisions its workspace afresh (the relaunch tests, and `workspace-init provision` on the real binary).

**The orphan sweep taking the swept issue's disk.** Same structure as the first: the sweep deleting the issue's Sandbox and pod is covered by the package's tests; the disk following the pod is the mechanism measured in round 1; the composition is unobserved.

**A kept pod keeping the same disk** (`kill-launcher`): the package tests cover that a launcher kill does not replace the pod, and the disk's identity follows from the pod not being replaced, but the uid equality itself is live-only.
coverageInventory.couldBeProvenHereButIsNot: One, and I closed it rather than report it: the uid comparison in the displacement window's stand-in (see `addedTest`). Nothing else in the seven is reachable here and left unreached.

findingsNotFailures.what: `docs/kubernetes.md:1316`, step 9 of the cutover this change writes: `kubectl -n legion get pvc -l legion.dev/project=<PROJECT>`, with the sentence that it "answers this question with silence whether the cutover worked or not".
findingsNotFailures.evidence: The label's value is the project token, not the project key: `bootreads.go:41` passes `claim.ProjectToken(cfg.Project)` into the runtime, and `claim/token.go` lower-cases and strips non-alphanumerics, so an operator substituting `INFRA` as the upper-case placeholder invites selects nothing — and the page pre-explains that silence as the expected outcome. The same page writes `<project>` lower-case at :1148, :1262 and :2825, and `legion.dev/issue=<KEY>` and `legion.dev/tree=<ROOT ISSUE>` are correctly upper-case (`labelValue`, names.go:273), so the two label families genuinely differ and a blanket sweep would break three working commands. Second, and not in the architect's report: with the **correct** value the command does not answer with silence either — each repository cache's claim template carries `legion.dev/project` (`repocache.go:96,116`) and, under `controller: daemon`, so does the controller's (`podkind.go:304`), so it returns exactly the exception claims step 9 then asks the operator to recognise.
findingsNotFailures.verdict: A finding to fix in this pull request, not a round failure, and that judgement is mine as the architect asked at 10:33Z. The step's actual audit instrument is the `jq` over every claim by owner that follows, which carries no label selector and is unaffected; no operator action goes wrong, and the wasted command costs one line. It is a sentence of explanation that is wrong in two ways, which is a fix of one placeholder and one clause, not a test round. I wrote no test for it: a test over documentation prose is the kind of source-text assertion that should not be pinned.

residualRisks: An issue pod's name is stable, so its ephemeral claim is always `<pod>-issue`; a replacement pod created before the predecessor's claim is reaped stays Pending until it is. Measured at about one second on a real cluster against a 120 s boot timeout, with `waitedOut` printing a Pending pod's events. Accepted as a risk by the architect.

A daemon that restarts inside the gap a migrating replacement opens has neither the Sandbox nor the runtime's kept name, and reads those roles' ends as deaths. The code says so in `replaceSupersededSandbox`'s own comment; the window is one delete-and-create of the cutover launch, and no test covers a daemon restart inside it because nothing here can restart a daemon mid-launch.
observations: The three repository files the sandbox package's tests read by relative path (`deploy/kubernetes/operator-route/pod.yml`, `packages/contracts/fixtures/dispatch-public-url.json`, `docs/kubernetes.md`) make the package unrunnable from a copy of `packages/daemon` alone. Not a defect — nothing runs it that way but a tester — but it is why my round-2 mutation evidence named a FAIL I could not attribute, and why this round I symlinked them beside the copy before trusting any mutation result.

Round 1's correction still stands: a label on the ephemeral claim template is pruned **with** a `warning: 299` header the daemon does not surface, so `podkind.go`'s "without a word" is one word too strong.
